claim_boundary: Themes and variable subthemes are derived from the baseline first-principles account and explicit paper-family boundary tests; this is not an official conference classification or prevalence estimate.
source_boundary: Concept definitions come from the baseline taxonomy. Subtheme boundaries are proposed from recurring ordinary pressures, failures, mechanisms, and evidence counts; paper membership is adjudicated separately.
membership_evidence_rule: D1 title-only records may propose candidates but cannot establish conceptual membership; D2 abstract evidence can establish a bounded speech object and problem; D3 full-paper evidence is required for mechanism and evaluation claims.

themes.name: Sound, bodies, rooms, and recording
themes.question: How does a human or other source turn a physical event into the signal a machine receives?
themes.ordinary_problem: Speech reaches a microphone as changing air pressure after vocal-fold vibration, mouth shape, room reflections, and electronics have already mixed together.
themes.naive_failure: Treating the waveform as an unstructured list of samples hides which changes came from the talker, the room, or the recording device.
themes.recurring_move: Separate source, filter, geometry, and time scale so a measured signal can be related back to a physical cause.
themes.tradeoff: A useful physical description can be wrong when bodies, rooms, or microphones violate its assumptions.

subthemes.name: Making a physical sound
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by making a physical sound, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The source and tract shape the pressure wave before a device records it.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Periodic vocal-fold source
concepts.definition: A speaker can repeatedly open and close the vocal folds; the repetition supplies pitch and harmonic energy while its exact timing varies.
concepts.boundary: Not every speech segment is periodic: frication, stops, breath, and irregular phonation cannot be reduced to one stable pitch.
concepts.positive_example: A study measures vocal-fold pulse timing or harmonic structure in voiced vowels.
concepts.negative_example: A study models only a microphone's frequency response with no source or phonation question.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Vocal-tract filtering
concepts.definition: The tongue, lips, jaw, and throat reshape source energy so some frequency regions are strengthened and others weakened; those regions carry much of vowel identity.
concepts.boundary: A filter-only explanation misses changes caused directly by source irregularity, radiation, or recording conditions.
concepts.positive_example: A study links tongue or lip geometry to vowel resonances or spectral peaks.
concepts.negative_example: A study predicts words from text without modeling how the tract shapes sound.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Coordinating moving speech parts
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by coordinating moving speech parts, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: Gesture overlap and timing are the object; a static source/filter description is not enough.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Articulatory coordination
concepts.definition: Speech is a timed coordination of several moving constrictions, not a sequence of isolated sounds; overlap lets one gesture affect its neighbors.
concepts.boundary: A label such as a phoneme is not itself a physical movement or a complete account of coarticulation.
concepts.positive_example: A study measures overlapping lip, tongue, jaw, or laryngeal gestures over time.
concepts.negative_example: A study treats each phoneme as an isolated label with no timing or movement evidence.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Representing a changing signal
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by representing a changing signal, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The question is what a digital representation keeps or loses across time, frequency, and precision.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Local frequency content
concepts.definition: Short windows expose which frequencies are present near each moment, making pitch, resonances, and noise easier to compare than raw samples alone.
concepts.boundary: A window discards some exact timing and long-range phase; two signals with similar spectra may still sound different.
concepts.positive_example: A spectrogram or short-time Fourier representation tracks local frequency content.
concepts.negative_example: A long-term average spectrum with no time-local measurement is not a windowed account.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Multiple time scales
concepts.definition: Fast events such as consonant closures and slow changes such as intonation require measurements at different temporal resolutions.
concepts.boundary: Adding resolutions is not automatically informative; it can increase computation or preserve nuisance variation.
concepts.positive_example: A method combines short windows for closures with longer windows for intonation or rhythm.
concepts.negative_example: Adding multiple neural layers without showing distinct time scales is not itself multi-resolution analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Sampling and quantization
concepts.definition: A digital recording keeps a finite set of amplitude measurements, so the sampling rate and numeric precision set what can still be recovered.
concepts.boundary: A high sample rate cannot restore information lost through clipping, poor microphones, or an absent frequency range.
concepts.positive_example: A study analyzes sample rate, bit depth, clipping, or quantization noise as information limits.
concepts.negative_example: A model that merely uses digital audio but never examines discretization does not instantiate this concept.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Changing the path from source to sensor
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by changing the path from source to sensor, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: Room reflections, device coloration, and alternate sensors change the evidence before recognition.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Reverberant room mixture
concepts.definition: The microphone hears direct sound plus delayed reflections, so a word can overlap its own earlier energy and blur boundaries.
concepts.boundary: Reverberation is not just additive stationary noise; its delay pattern depends on room geometry and position.
concepts.positive_example: A method separates direct speech from delayed room reflections or models room impulse responses.
concepts.negative_example: Stationary additive microphone hiss with no room-delay structure is not reverberant mixing.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Microphone and channel coloration
concepts.definition: A device emphasizes some frequencies, clips loud peaks, or transmits only a narrow band, changing the evidence available to a recognizer.
concepts.boundary: Channel normalization can remove useful speaker or environment information along with nuisance coloration.
concepts.positive_example: A system corrects frequency coloration, clipping, bandwidth, or device-specific transmission effects.
concepts.negative_example: A speaker adaptation method that never observes a recording channel is not channel modeling.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Non-airborne speech sensing
concepts.definition: Neck vibration, ultrasound, radar, or muscle signals can observe speech when airborne audio is missing, but they observe a different projection of the act.
concepts.boundary: A sensor that works in quiet laboratory placement is not automatically a replacement for ordinary audio in daily use.
concepts.positive_example: Speech is inferred from neck vibration, ultrasound, radar, or another non-airborne sensor.
concepts.negative_example: Ordinary far-field microphone speech, even if noisy, is not non-airborne sensing.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: Listening through noise, overlap, and missing sound
themes.question: How can a system recover one useful speech stream from several competing or damaged signals?
themes.ordinary_problem: A listener often hears several talkers, music, echo, and device noise at once, yet needs one person's words or an intelligible mixture.
themes.naive_failure: Amplifying everything or subtracting an average noise profile also removes quiet consonants and fails when the interferer changes with the speech.
themes.recurring_move: Use structure that differs between target and interference—time, frequency, space, source identity, or learned speech regularity—to estimate and reconstruct the target.
themes.tradeoff: A cleaner waveform may be less faithful, introduce artifacts, or favor the wrong speaker when the mixture is ambiguous.

subthemes.name: Suppressing changing interference
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by suppressing changing interference, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The target is one speech stream and the failure is removing speech along with noise.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Time-frequency masking
concepts.definition: Estimate how much each local frequency region belongs to speech, then attenuate regions dominated by noise.
concepts.boundary: A binary or soft mask can create musical noise and cannot reliably separate sources that occupy the same region.
concepts.positive_example: A system estimates a time-frequency mask and attenuates bins assigned to noise.
concepts.negative_example: A waveform denoiser with no time-frequency assignment is not necessarily masking.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Speech-prior denoising
concepts.definition: A model learned from clean speech can fill in a plausible speech pattern where the recording is noisy, trading exact fidelity for intelligibility.
concepts.boundary: A plausible completion can hallucinate phonetic detail the microphone never captured.
concepts.positive_example: A learned clean-speech prior reconstructs plausible speech where noise obscures the waveform.
concepts.negative_example: A fixed notch filter that uses no speech structure is not a speech prior.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Changing and adverse noise
concepts.definition: The useful distinction is whether noise changes faster than the system can track, as with competing speech, vehicles, or sudden events.
concepts.boundary: A result on fixed background noise does not establish performance under changing or speech-like interference.
concepts.positive_example: The interference changes rapidly or contains competing speech, feedback, or transient events.
concepts.negative_example: A single fixed broadband noise condition does not establish nonstationary-noise handling.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Recovering several hidden sources
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by recovering several hidden sources, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The mixture contains multiple sources and the system must infer source identity or count.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Blind source separation
concepts.definition: Infer several hidden signals from their mixture using differences in statistics, timing, or spectral structure without receiving isolated sources at test time.
concepts.boundary: The mixture may not contain enough information to identify sources uniquely; permutation and source-count assumptions matter.
concepts.positive_example: Several hidden signals are inferred from their mixture without isolated target audio at test time.
concepts.negative_example: A target voice embedding supplied at test time makes the task target-conditioned rather than blind.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Target-conditioned separation
concepts.definition: A voice example, enrollment identity, or visual cue tells the separator which source to preserve rather than asking it to output every source.
concepts.boundary: Conditioning can lock onto the wrong talker or encode identity without guaranteeing intelligible content.
concepts.positive_example: An enrollment voice, visual cue, or target example selects which speaker to retain.
concepts.negative_example: Separating every source without a target condition is not target-conditioned separation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Using location to select sound
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by using location to select sound, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: Microphone geometry and direction are the evidence; a single-channel separator has a different limit.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Spatial filtering
concepts.definition: Several microphones provide direction-dependent differences, allowing a filter to reinforce one location and reject others.
concepts.boundary: A single microphone or moving speaker removes the spatial cue the method depends on.
concepts.positive_example: Microphone-array direction or spatial covariance is used to reinforce one location.
concepts.negative_example: A single-channel spectral model with no spatial input is not spatial filtering.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Canceling copies and filling gaps
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by canceling copies and filling gaps, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The unwanted signal is a known delayed copy or missing frame, not an arbitrary background.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Acoustic echo cancellation
concepts.definition: Use the known far-end playback signal to predict the speaker signal that returns through the room, then subtract that predicted copy.
concepts.boundary: The loudspeaker path changes with movement and delay; an imperfect estimate can cancel near-end speech.
concepts.positive_example: Known loudspeaker playback is used to estimate and subtract its reflected copy from microphone input.
concepts.negative_example: Removing unrelated background noise without a playback reference is not echo cancellation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Packet-loss concealment
concepts.definition: When transmitted audio frames disappear, infer a short continuation from nearby waveform or speech structure so playback does not break.
concepts.boundary: Short plausible continuation is not recovery of the original utterance and becomes unsafe over long gaps.
concepts.positive_example: Missing transmitted frames are filled using neighboring waveform or speech continuity.
concepts.negative_example: Denoising a complete recording is not packet-loss concealment.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Optimizing what a listener can use
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by optimizing what a listener can use, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: This boundary is for methods whose target is what a listener can understand or tolerate; it is separate from noise removal, separation, and packet repair, which target a signal or source before the listener judges it.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Perceptual enhancement
concepts.definition: Optimize what a listener can understand or tolerate rather than preserving every sample, using intelligibility or quality as the target.
concepts.boundary: A perceptual score can hide distortions important for recognition, speaker identity, or forensic use.
concepts.positive_example: Enhancement is optimized or judged by intelligibility, listener quality, or perceptual acceptability.
concepts.negative_example: A lower sample MSE alone is not perceptual enhancement evidence.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: From sound to words and structured speech
themes.question: How does a system turn a continuous acoustic stream into the words, boundaries, and disfluencies a user meant?
themes.ordinary_problem: Speech has no visible spaces between words, and pronunciation, speed, accent, noise, and hesitation vary even when the intended sentence is the same.
themes.naive_failure: Matching each sound to a fixed dictionary pronunciation or treating the utterance as already segmented fails on coarticulation, new words, and disfluency.
themes.recurring_move: Infer a sequence of linguistic units while allowing uncertainty about boundaries, pronunciation, context, and what should be preserved.
themes.tradeoff: A fluent transcript can be easier to read but less faithful to what was said, including omissions, hesitation, or uncertainty.

subthemes.name: Learning reusable sound units
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by learning reusable sound units, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The system first decides what reusable evidence can be extracted from continuous sound.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Acoustic-to-token mapping
concepts.definition: The system scores candidate symbol sequences against the observed sound and chooses or represents alternatives rather than reading words directly from samples.
concepts.boundary: The highest-scoring sequence may exploit dataset regularities instead of matching the actual speech.
concepts.positive_example: A continuous acoustic sequence is scored against phones, words, or discrete recognition tokens.
concepts.negative_example: Text-only language modeling with no acoustic input is not acoustic-to-token mapping.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Learned speech units
concepts.definition: Predicting or grouping parts of unlabeled audio can provide reusable units before a task-specific word recognizer is trained.
concepts.boundary: A useful pretraining prediction need not produce units aligned with words, phonemes, or human categories.
concepts.positive_example: Unlabeled speech predicts masked or neighboring content to create reusable acoustic representations.
concepts.negative_example: A supervised classifier trained only on labeled words is not self-supervised unit learning.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Allowing different realizations of words
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by allowing different realizations of words, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The same intended unit has multiple acoustic paths; this is distinct from learning a unit representation.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Pronunciation variation
concepts.definition: The same word can have reductions, substitutions, or accent-specific realizations, so recognition must allow more than one acoustic path.
concepts.boundary: Adding variants without evidence can increase confusions and may encode an accent as an error.
concepts.positive_example: Recognition explicitly permits reductions, substitutions, accents, or multiple pronunciations of a word.
concepts.negative_example: Adding a new vocabulary item without pronunciation variation is not this concept.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Locating units in time
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by locating units in time, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The output must preserve or locate timing, hesitation, repair, or sequence boundaries.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Temporal alignment
concepts.definition: Align an audio timeline with words, phones, or labels so duration and position can be measured rather than treating the utterance as an unordered bag.
concepts.boundary: Forced alignment assumes the transcript is correct and can conceal recognition errors.
concepts.positive_example: Words, phones, or labels are assigned positions and durations on an audio timeline.
concepts.negative_example: An utterance-level class with no temporal correspondence is not alignment.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Disfluency and event preservation
concepts.definition: Represent pauses, repetitions, repairs, laughter, and overlap when those events are part of the communication or the clinical signal.
concepts.boundary: Removing them may improve readability while destroying evidence needed for conversation analysis or diagnosis.
concepts.positive_example: Pauses, repetitions, repairs, laughter, or overlap are retained as output events.
concepts.negative_example: Cleaning a transcript by deleting all disfluencies is the neighboring failure, not preservation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Using context without inventing words
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by using context without inventing words, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: Context, speaker evidence, and new words resolve ambiguity but can override what was actually said.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Long-context decoding
concepts.definition: Use words and turns before and after a sound to resolve locally ambiguous acoustics, such as homophones or clipped endings.
concepts.boundary: Context can override a rare but correct word, especially when the language model has a strong prior.
concepts.positive_example: Earlier or later words and turns resolve an acoustically ambiguous local segment.
concepts.negative_example: A frame-local classifier that never uses surrounding context is not long-context decoding.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Domain and context biasing
concepts.definition: Use the meeting topic, contact list, or application vocabulary to raise plausible rare words without changing the audio itself.
concepts.boundary: A biased vocabulary can turn uncertainty into confident but context-shaped substitutions.
concepts.positive_example: A meeting topic, contact list, or application vocabulary changes rare-word decoding.
concepts.negative_example: A generic language model with no task context is not contextual biasing.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Speaker adaptation
concepts.definition: Adjust the acoustic or decoding assumptions to a talker's voice, speaking rate, or pronunciation using a small amount of evidence.
concepts.boundary: Adaptation can overfit a short sample and degrade when the talker changes state or the enrollment is wrong.
concepts.positive_example: A small enrollment sample changes acoustic or decoding assumptions for a particular talker.
concepts.negative_example: A single population-wide model with no speaker evidence is not adaptation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Open-vocabulary recognition
concepts.definition: Handle names, code-switching, jargon, and newly encountered words without requiring a fixed closed list.
concepts.boundary: Open vocabulary expands recall but makes spelling, segmentation, and evaluation less settled.
concepts.positive_example: The recognizer handles names, jargon, code-switching, or newly encountered words outside a fixed list.
concepts.negative_example: A closed command grammar with a fixed word list is not open-vocabulary recognition.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: From spoken form to meaning and coordinated action
themes.question: What does an utterance mean here, and what should another participant do with it?
themes.ordinary_problem: The same words can request, question, joke, refuse, or warn depending on prosody, shared history, timing, and the surrounding situation.
themes.naive_failure: A transcript-only system treats words as the whole message and misses intent, reference, turn structure, and what is appropriate to do next.
themes.recurring_move: Combine linguistic content with speaker, discourse history, prosody, visual or environmental context, and an explicit action or response target.
themes.tradeoff: More context can resolve ambiguity but can also leak private information, over-interpret the speaker, or make a system confidently act on a wrong inference.

subthemes.name: Meaning carried by how speech sounds
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by meaning carried by how speech sounds, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: This boundary covers information carried by pitch, timing, loudness, voice quality, or effort beyond the words; it is separate from dialogue action because the cue is in how an utterance sounds, not in the conversational state alone.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Prosodic meaning
concepts.definition: Pitch movement, timing, stress, and pauses can mark questions, contrast, turn completion, urgency, or attitude.
concepts.boundary: Prosody is language- and speaker-dependent; a pitch pattern is not a universal emotion label.
concepts.positive_example: Pitch, stress, rhythm, or pauses change whether an utterance sounds like a question, contrast, or turn completion.
concepts.negative_example: A lexical-only text classifier with no prosodic evidence is not prosodic meaning analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Paralinguistic state
concepts.definition: Voice properties can provide clues about emotion, fatigue, engagement, or health that are not the literal linguistic content.
concepts.boundary: A correlational acoustic cue is not proof of an internal state or a reliable diagnosis.
concepts.positive_example: Acoustic voice changes are used as clues about emotion, fatigue, engagement, or health.
concepts.negative_example: A diagnosis asserted from a transcript alone is not acoustic paralinguistic-state evidence.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Inferring what a speaker is trying to do
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by inferring what a speaker is trying to do, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The system tracks goals, commitments, and situation rather than only classifying acoustic style.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Intent in context
concepts.definition: Infer what the speaker is trying to accomplish from words plus the situation and prior turns, then keep uncertainty when several intents fit.
concepts.boundary: Intent labels often reflect annotator interpretation and may erase ambiguity or culturally different readings.
concepts.positive_example: Words, prosody, and discourse situation jointly determine whether a speaker requests, warns, jokes, or refuses.
concepts.negative_example: Assigning intent from isolated keywords alone is not context-sensitive intent inference.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Dialogue state
concepts.definition: Track unresolved questions, commitments, entities, and prior actions so a response is connected to the conversation rather than only the last sentence.
concepts.boundary: A stored state can be stale, incorrectly inferred, or sensitive, and the system may not know when to discard it.
concepts.positive_example: The system tracks unresolved questions, commitments, entities, and prior actions across turns.
concepts.negative_example: A response based only on the last utterance is not dialogue-state tracking.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Coordinating participation under uncertainty
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by coordinating participation under uncertainty, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The problem is when to speak, yield, interrupt, or ask for clarification.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Turn-boundary prediction
concepts.definition: Predict whether a speaker is continuing, yielding, or likely to stop so a system can respond without cutting them off.
concepts.boundary: A pause is not always a turn end; cultures, speakers, and task types change timing conventions.
concepts.positive_example: The system predicts whether a speaker will continue, yield, or stop before responding.
concepts.negative_example: Detecting sentence punctuation after the turn is complete is not turn-boundary prediction.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Repair and clarification
concepts.definition: When recognition or understanding is uncertain, ask a targeted question or offer alternatives instead of silently continuing.
concepts.boundary: A clarification costs time and can burden users if uncertainty estimates are poorly calibrated.
concepts.positive_example: Uncertainty triggers a targeted question, confirmation, or alternative instead of silent continuation.
concepts.negative_example: Returning a confident guess without a correction path is not repair.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Connecting language to a shared world
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by connecting language to a shared world, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: A phrase must identify a referent or authorized action and remain corrigible through feedback.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Referential grounding
concepts.definition: Use the scene, shared task, or prior mention to determine which object, person, or event a phrase denotes.
concepts.boundary: Words alone may underdetermine the referent; a model can infer a plausible object without actually observing it.
concepts.positive_example: A phrase such as 'that cup' is linked to an object in the shared scene or prior discourse.
concepts.negative_example: Choosing a likely object without scene or discourse evidence is not grounding.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Speech act
concepts.definition: Distinguish information from a request, command, permission, or commitment because the same proposition can require different responses.
concepts.boundary: Classifying an act does not grant authority to execute it.
concepts.positive_example: The system distinguishes an assertion from a request, command, permission, or commitment.
concepts.negative_example: Topic classification without an action or authority interpretation is not speech-act analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Interactional feedback
concepts.definition: Let user corrections, confirmations, and response outcomes update the system's interpretation during the interaction.
concepts.boundary: Feedback can be sparse, ambiguous, or shaped by users adapting to the system's mistakes.
concepts.positive_example: User correction or response outcome updates what the system believes the user meant.
concepts.negative_example: Logging a prediction without using subsequent interaction is not feedback.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: Creating speech while keeping the right things fixed
themes.question: How can a system produce intelligible speech while controlling content, identity, timing, style, and naturalness separately?
themes.ordinary_problem: A useful synthetic voice must say the requested content, sound like the intended speaker or style, and remain understandable as it changes over time.
themes.naive_failure: Copying a recording or predicting samples directly entangles words with identity, pitch, rhythm, and recording conditions, making controlled change difficult.
themes.recurring_move: Represent or condition distinct factors, generate a time-consistent waveform or acoustic sequence, and evaluate each requested property separately.
themes.tradeoff: Factor separation is rarely perfect: changing identity can change content, style controls can sound artificial, and a plausible voice can be misused.

subthemes.name: Turning language into a timed speech plan
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by turning language into a timed speech plan, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: This boundary covers the step from intended text or meaning to pronunciation, duration, pitch targets, and sequence; it is separate from waveform generation, which realizes an already chosen plan as samples.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Text-to-speech planning
concepts.definition: Choose pronunciation, durations, pitch targets, and acoustic details before or while producing the waveform so written content becomes speakable.
concepts.boundary: Text does not specify one correct prosody, and a fluent output can still mispronounce names or sound unnatural.
concepts.positive_example: Text is converted into pronunciation, duration, pitch, and acoustic plans before waveform generation.
concepts.negative_example: A waveform vocoder receiving a complete acoustic plan is not itself text-to-speech planning.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Producing or compressing audible detail
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by producing or compressing audible detail, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The issue is sample-level detail and the tradeoff between faithful content and natural sound.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Waveform synthesis
concepts.definition: Generate fine-grained samples conditioned on a coarser acoustic plan, reconstructing the periodic and noisy detail listeners hear as voice.
concepts.boundary: Sample-level realism does not guarantee correct words, stable identity, or natural long-range timing.
concepts.positive_example: A model generates fine waveform samples conditioned on a lower-rate acoustic representation.
concepts.negative_example: A text-to-text model with no waveform synthesis is not a neural vocoder.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Intelligibility versus naturalness
concepts.definition: Treat ease of understanding and human-likeness as related but distinct targets that need separate tests.
concepts.boundary: A single listener score can conflate content accuracy, recording quality, and preference.
concepts.positive_example: Separate tests ask whether words are understood and whether the voice sounds human-like.
concepts.negative_example: One unqualified quality score cannot establish both intelligibility and naturalness.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Changing who sounds like the speaker
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by changing who sounds like the speaker, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: This boundary covers changing or measuring who the voice sounds like while keeping the message stable; it is separate from expression control, which changes emotion or style, and from content planning, which changes the speech plan.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Speaker identity representation
concepts.definition: Capture stable voice traits that let a system preserve or imitate who is speaking across different words and sessions.
concepts.boundary: A short recording can encode noise, emotion, or demographic stereotypes rather than stable identity.
concepts.positive_example: A representation preserves or imitates a person's stable vocal characteristics across words.
concepts.negative_example: A recording-specific noise signature mistaken for identity is not a valid identity representation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Voice conversion
concepts.definition: Transform the acoustic realization toward a target voice while trying to preserve linguistic timing and content.
concepts.boundary: Conversion may leak source identity, distort pronunciation, or require target-speaker data unavailable in practice.
concepts.positive_example: The acoustic realization moves toward a target speaker while the source linguistic content remains.
concepts.negative_example: Changing text content without preserving the source message is not voice conversion.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Unseen-speaker synthesis
concepts.definition: Use a voice description or brief enrollment to synthesize a speaker not represented by a dedicated model.
concepts.boundary: Similarity on a benchmark does not establish consent, identity security, or robustness to unusual voices.
concepts.positive_example: A brief enrollment or description synthesizes a speaker without a dedicated per-speaker model.
concepts.negative_example: A model trained and tested only on speakers seen during training is not zero-shot voice.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Changing style, timing, and response behavior
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by changing style, timing, and response behavior, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The system must obey expressive controls quickly without breaking continuity or meaning.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Prosody control
concepts.definition: Set or predict pitch, duration, energy, and pauses so the same words can sound questioning, emphatic, calm, or urgent.
concepts.boundary: Independent controls can conflict; expressive variation may change perceived meaning or naturalness.
concepts.positive_example: A user or model sets pitch, timing, energy, or pauses while keeping words fixed.
concepts.negative_example: Changing speaker identity without an explicit timing or melody control is not prosody control.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Style and emotion control
concepts.definition: Condition generation on a speaking style or affective target while preserving the requested content.
concepts.boundary: Emotion categories are culturally and contextually unstable, and a label may not describe what listeners perceive.
concepts.positive_example: A generation system is conditioned on a style or affect target while preserving content.
concepts.negative_example: A classifier that only labels emotion but generates nothing is not style control.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Interactive generation latency
concepts.definition: Produce speech quickly enough for a conversation while preserving continuity and allowing interruption or correction.
concepts.boundary: Low latency can require shorter context, lower quality, or speculative output that must later be repaired.
concepts.positive_example: A voice system speaks quickly, permits interruption, and responds within conversational timing.
concepts.negative_example: Offline synthesis with no response-time or interruption constraint is not interactive latency work.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: Speakers as changing people, not nuisance variables
themes.question: How should speech systems represent differences between people and changes within one person?
themes.ordinary_problem: Voice depends on anatomy, age, health, emotion, language history, social setting, and equipment; these differences affect both communication and measurement.
themes.naive_failure: Treating variation as noise makes systems work best for a narrow population and can turn a health or identity signal into an unwanted demographic shortcut.
themes.recurring_move: Measure which variation is task-relevant, model it explicitly when appropriate, and test performance and meaning across people and conditions.
themes.tradeoff: A factor that helps prediction may be sensitive, confounded, or harmful to expose; personalization can improve access while increasing privacy risk.

subthemes.name: Identity, age, and changing voice
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by identity, age, and changing voice, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The evidence concerns who is speaking and how that person's voice changes across time and state.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Speaker verification
concepts.definition: Decide whether two recordings plausibly came from the same person under channel, time, and content variation.
concepts.boundary: Similarity scores are not identity proof and depend on enrollment quality, population, and decision threshold.
concepts.positive_example: Two recordings are compared to decide whether they came from the same person.
concepts.negative_example: Predicting age or emotion without comparing identity is not speaker verification.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Age and developmental speech
concepts.definition: Children and older adults differ in anatomy, articulation, vocabulary, and interaction needs, so adult data is not a neutral reference.
concepts.boundary: Age prediction or age normalization can encode stereotypes and may not address the actual recognition failure.
concepts.positive_example: A system models children or older adults whose anatomy, language, or interaction differs from adults.
concepts.negative_example: A generic adult corpus with age omitted is not age/development analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Within-speaker state variation
concepts.definition: The same person's voice shifts with fatigue, emotion, health, audience, and speaking effort; robust systems must not confuse state with identity.
concepts.boundary: There is no universal stable identity vector independent of context.
concepts.positive_example: The same speaker is measured across fatigue, emotion, effort, audience, or health states.
concepts.negative_example: Differences only between unrelated speakers are not within-speaker state variation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Speech measurements associated with health
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by speech measurements associated with health, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: A measurable speech property is evaluated as a possible health signal, with clinical limits kept explicit.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Clinical speech marker
concepts.definition: Measure a reproducible speech property associated with a clinical condition or progression, while separating it from age, device, and language effects.
concepts.boundary: Association with a diagnosis is not clinical validity, causation, or permission to make a medical decision.
concepts.positive_example: A reproducible pause, articulation, or voice measure is tested against a clinical condition or severity scale.
concepts.negative_example: A speech feature correlated with a generic class but never tied to a clinical target is not a clinical marker.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Communicating with atypical or impaired speech
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by communicating with atypical or impaired speech, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The goal is recognition or expression for people whose speech does not match majority training data.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Atypical articulation and dysarthria
concepts.definition: Recognize or synthesize speech whose timing, precision, or coordination differs from training norms instead of treating it as mere noise.
concepts.boundary: Small datasets and speaker-specific patterns make broad claims especially fragile.
concepts.positive_example: Recognition or synthesis explicitly handles atypical timing, precision, or coordination.
concepts.negative_example: Treating all low-confidence speech as atypical without a speaker or disorder target is not this concept.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Augmentative communication
concepts.definition: Use residual vocal, muscular, visual, or typed signals to help a person express intended language or control a device.
concepts.boundary: A system should preserve the person's authorship and offer correction, not silently decide what they meant.
concepts.positive_example: Residual vocal, muscular, visual, or typed signals are turned into a person's intended communication.
concepts.negative_example: A general speech recognizer for fluent speakers is not augmentative communication.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Whether the system actually helps a person
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by whether the system actually helps a person, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The target is effort, control, access, and fit in a real activity rather than model accuracy alone.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Listener effort
concepts.definition: Measure how much concentration, repetition, or repair a listener needs, not just whether a word error count changed.
concepts.boundary: Effort measures depend on task, listener experience, and presentation conditions.
concepts.positive_example: Listeners' concentration, repetition, or effort is measured under a speech condition.
concepts.negative_example: WER alone, with no listener task or report, is not listener-effort evidence.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: User control and consent
concepts.definition: Let speakers decide how their voice is recorded, adapted, generated, shared, or corrected, especially when identity is involved.
concepts.boundary: A consent checkbox does not solve power imbalance, downstream copying, or inability to withdraw a trained model.
concepts.positive_example: A system gives people control over recording, adaptation, generation, sharing, or correction of their voice.
concepts.negative_example: A privacy statement with no user choice or withdrawal path is not demonstrated control.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Accessibility fit
concepts.definition: Judge whether a system works within a person's actual device, environment, communication practice, and time constraints.
concepts.boundary: A lab improvement can be irrelevant or harmful if setup, latency, or interaction burden is omitted.
concepts.positive_example: Evaluation includes the person's actual device, environment, communication practice, setup burden, or timing needs.
concepts.negative_example: A clean laboratory score with no user or deployment constraint is not accessibility fit.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: Many languages, accents, and unequal evidence
themes.question: How can speech technology serve people whose language or variety has little labeled data or little institutional support?
themes.ordinary_problem: Languages differ in sounds, writing systems, grammar, prosody, code-switching, and social meaning; data and tools are distributed unevenly.
themes.naive_failure: Scaling an English-centered recipe or translating labels assumes that all languages expose the same units, data, and errors.
themes.recurring_move: Share useful structure across languages while preserving language-specific distinctions, measuring who benefits, and making uncertainty visible where evidence is thin.
themes.tradeoff: Transfer can import pronunciation or cultural assumptions, and aggregate multilingual scores can hide severe failures in a small language or community.

subthemes.name: Sharing structure across languages
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by sharing structure across languages, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The central question is what can be shared while retaining language-specific distinctions.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Cross-lingual transfer
concepts.definition: Reuse representations or training signals from one language to improve another when their speech structure overlaps.
concepts.boundary: Transfer may favor high-resource languages and erase distinctions absent from the source language.
concepts.positive_example: Training signals or representations from one language improve another language while measuring what is lost.
concepts.negative_example: Translating an English label without cross-language speech evidence is not cross-lingual transfer.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Language and variety identification
concepts.definition: Determine which language or variety is being spoken so the appropriate recognizer or interaction policy can be selected.
concepts.boundary: Closely related varieties and code-switching make a single label inadequate or politically loaded.
concepts.positive_example: The system selects a language or variety from spoken input before choosing a downstream policy.
concepts.negative_example: Classifying topics or speakers without language choice is not language identification.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Code-switching
concepts.definition: Handle a speaker moving between languages within an utterance, including pronunciation, grammar, and word-boundary changes.
concepts.boundary: A monolingual metric can count appropriate switching as error and fail to define the intended transcript.
concepts.positive_example: A single utterance changes language and the recognizer preserves its words, boundaries, and pronunciation shifts.
concepts.negative_example: Separate monolingual recordings are not code-switching.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Learning from sparse labels
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by learning from sparse labels, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The method changes how a model learns when labeled examples are scarce.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Self-training
concepts.definition: Use a model's predictions on unlabeled speech as additional training signals, ideally filtering or weighting uncertain labels.
concepts.boundary: Errors can reinforce themselves and create a false appearance of data scale.
concepts.positive_example: A model labels unlabeled speech and filtered predictions become new training examples.
concepts.negative_example: Adding more human-transcribed data is not self-training.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Few-shot adaptation
concepts.definition: Adjust a model to a language, speaker, or domain from a small number of examples rather than retraining from scratch.
concepts.boundary: Few examples may cover only one speaker or style and make variance look like progress.
concepts.positive_example: A model changes to a new language, speaker, or domain from only a small number of examples.
concepts.negative_example: A full retraining run on a large new corpus is not few-shot adaptation.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Making missing speech evidence
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by making missing speech evidence, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The work creates speakers, prompts, labels, or recordings needed by a community or task.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Speech data collection
concepts.definition: Design recording prompts, speakers, transcription, and consent so newly collected data covers the intended community and task.
concepts.boundary: More hours do not fix biased sampling, poor transcripts, or a task definition that excludes natural speech.
concepts.positive_example: A study designs prompts, speakers, transcripts, permissions, and sampling for a new speech corpus.
concepts.negative_example: Using an existing benchmark without examining its collection is not data-collection analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Respecting variation and local meaning
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by respecting variation and local meaning, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: This boundary covers differences in pronunciation, variety, and local meaning that affect who is understood and how speech is interpreted; it is separate from generic low-resource learning because more data alone cannot decide whether a social or cultural distinction was represented correctly.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Accent robustness
concepts.definition: Maintain intended-word accuracy across pronunciation patterns that differ from the training majority.
concepts.boundary: A single pooled error rate cannot show which accents fail or whether adaptation changes identity representation.
concepts.positive_example: Intended-word accuracy is measured across pronunciation patterns outside the training majority.
concepts.negative_example: A pooled score with no accent or variety breakdown is not evidence of accent robustness.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Dialect and variety
concepts.definition: Treat grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and discourse conventions of a variety as part of the language, not merely deviations from a standard.
concepts.boundary: Dialect labels can be contested and may conflate region, ethnicity, class, and speaker identity.
concepts.positive_example: A study treats a community's pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, or discourse as a language variety.
concepts.negative_example: Calling every deviation from a standard an error is the boundary failure, not dialect analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Cultural meaning
concepts.definition: Interpret politeness, indirectness, emotion, and conversational norms within the community that uses them.
concepts.boundary: A label imported from another culture may be statistically convenient but semantically wrong.
concepts.positive_example: Interpretation is evaluated against community-specific politeness, indirectness, emotion, or conversational norms.
concepts.negative_example: Importing a label from another culture without local interpretation is not cultural-meaning analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

themes.name: Evidence, practical systems, and consequences
themes.question: What does a result establish, under what conditions, and who is affected when the system leaves the paper?
themes.ordinary_problem: Speech systems are used through microphones, networks, interfaces, policies, and people; a benchmark number is only one observation of that whole chain.
themes.naive_failure: Reporting one average score on one dataset encourages the reader to treat a proxy as universal ability and ignores latency, failure recovery, privacy, and misuse.
themes.recurring_move: Align the evaluation with the real target, expose subgroup and condition variation, account for the full system boundary, and preserve an audit trail from evidence to claim.
themes.tradeoff: Broader evaluation costs time and data, but narrow evidence can create false confidence exactly where speech systems affect access, identity, or safety.

subthemes.name: Connecting scores to human goals
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by connecting scores to human goals, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: A metric is a proxy and must be tied to the human or engineering property it represents.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Word error versus understanding
concepts.definition: A transcript edit distance counts substitutions, insertions, and deletions, but a small count is not automatically successful task understanding.
concepts.boundary: A word metric can miss critical entity errors and can penalize harmless orthographic or dialect differences.
concepts.positive_example: A paper compares transcript edit distance with whether a person can complete the intended task or recover critical entities.
concepts.negative_example: Reporting WER and calling it understanding without a task measure is not this concept.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Quality and naturalness
concepts.definition: Listening ratings, preference tests, and signal measures estimate different aspects of whether generated or enhanced speech is acceptable.
concepts.boundary: A score without listeners, conditions, and target definition cannot support a general quality claim.
concepts.positive_example: Listeners or a defined signal target judge acceptability, preference, naturalness, or intelligibility under stated conditions.
concepts.negative_example: An unexplained aggregate score with no target or listening condition is not quality evidence.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Calibration and selective use
concepts.definition: A system should know when its uncertainty is high enough to defer, ask, or show alternatives rather than making every output look certain.
concepts.boundary: Calibration on a held-out sample does not guarantee safety under a new population or distribution.
concepts.positive_example: A system defers, asks, or shows alternatives when confidence does not match observed correctness.
concepts.negative_example: A softmax score reported without reliability or selective behavior is not calibration.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Changing speakers, rooms, and conditions
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by changing speakers, rooms, and conditions, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The question is whether failures are detected and recovered when conditions differ from training.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Distribution shift
concepts.definition: Performance changes when speakers, microphones, rooms, languages, topics, or noise differ from training and test conditions.
concepts.boundary: A named shift is not evidence of coverage; the shift must be measured and tied to the failure.
concepts.positive_example: The same system is tested across new speakers, rooms, microphones, languages, topics, or noise conditions.
concepts.negative_example: Calling a dataset diverse without measuring a train-test change is not distribution-shift evidence.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: End-to-end recovery
concepts.definition: Handle uncertainty through confirmation, correction, fallback, and logging so one recognition error does not become an irreversible action.
concepts.boundary: A robust component is not an end-to-end safe system if downstream policy ignores its uncertainty.
concepts.positive_example: A recognition error leads to confirmation, correction, fallback, or logging instead of irreversible action.
concepts.negative_example: Improving one model component without testing downstream recovery is not end-to-end recovery.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Meeting time, memory, and hardware limits
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by meeting time, memory, and hardware limits, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: The system must operate within a device or interaction budget without hiding cost elsewhere.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Latency and resource budget
concepts.definition: A system must meet timing, memory, energy, bandwidth, and hardware limits while preserving the property users need.
concepts.boundary: A faster model may emit less context, reduce quality, or move cost into an unreported service.
concepts.positive_example: A paper measures response time, memory, energy, bandwidth, or compute under a deployment constraint.
concepts.negative_example: A smaller parameter count with no resource or timing measurement is not a deployment-budget result.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Protecting voice and resisting misuse
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by protecting voice and resisting misuse, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: This boundary covers harm from exposing voice identity or accepting imitation, replay, or generated speech as genuine; it is separate from ordinary robustness because the failure is unauthorized inference or deception, not merely a lower score in a changed condition.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Voice privacy
concepts.definition: Speech recordings reveal content and may reveal identity, health, location, emotion, or group membership, so collection and storage are part of the technical problem.
concepts.boundary: Removing words does not necessarily remove speaker identity or sensitive acoustic information.
concepts.positive_example: A system limits or audits what identity, health, location, or content can be inferred from recorded speech.
concepts.negative_example: Deleting the transcript while retaining identifiable acoustic recordings is not voice privacy.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

concepts.name: Spoofing and synthetic voice misuse
concepts.definition: A system must distinguish authorized speech from replayed or generated audio when identity or access depends on it.
concepts.boundary: A detector trained on known generators can fail on unseen synthesis, replay channels, or an attacker who changes the interaction.
concepts.positive_example: A detector tests replayed or generated speech against an identity or access decision, including unseen attacks.
concepts.negative_example: A normal speech classifier with no adversarial or synthetic-audio threat model is not spoofing analysis.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.

subthemes.name: Keeping claims inspectable and contestable
subthemes.question: What ordinary speech pressure is handled by keeping claims inspectable and contestable, and what evidence distinguishes it from neighboring pressures?
subthemes.derivation_boundary: A person must be able to trace evidence, uncertainty, and correction when a speech system matters.
subthemes.derivation_evidence: Split or retained because the ordinary pressure, failure mode, mechanism, or evaluation target differs from neighboring groups.

concepts.name: Auditability and contestability
concepts.definition: Keep enough provenance, uncertainty, and correction path for a person to understand and challenge a consequential speech-derived decision.
concepts.boundary: A stored confidence number is not an explanation of what evidence drove the decision.
concepts.positive_example: A consequential speech-derived decision preserves provenance, uncertainty, and a way for a person to challenge it.
concepts.negative_example: A confidence number without evidence trace or appeal path is not auditability.
concepts.membership_evidence_rule: D2 abstract evidence must name the spoken-speech object and conceptual pressure; D3 full-paper evidence must additionally support the mechanism and evaluation object.
